They may present as diffuse peritoneal implants, omental caking, mesenteric deposits, serosal bowel involvement, ascites, or multifocal adhesions and tumor-related tethering. In the emergency setting, these mechanisms can cause malignant bowel obstruction (MBO) at the gastric outlet, small bowel, large bowel, or multiple levels. Obstruction may result from extrinsic compression, serosal encasement, mesenteric shortening, intramural infiltration, impaired motility, or a combination of malignant and benign postoperative factors. Consequently, diagnostic work-up must not only confirm obstruction but also distinguish malignant from benign causes, map the number and site of transition points, and identify time-critical complications such as ischemia, perforation, closed-loop obstruction, or volvulus.

PSM has historically been regarded as end-stage disease with limited therapeutic options. Over the past two decades, however, advances in cytoreductive surgery (CRS), systemic treatment, and intraperitoneal chemotherapy have improved outcomes in selected patients [ 1 ]. In contrast, the management of surgical emergencies in patients with PSM remains poorly standardized, with wide variation across institutions and disciplines. These patients often present with substantial tumor burden, malnutrition, prior operations, ascites, and treatment-related physiological compromise, all of which amplify perioperative risk and complicate decision-making in the acute setting [ 2 ]. The lack of shared pathways and dedicated guidance may lead to both overtreatment and undertreatment [ 3 , 4 ].

To address this gap, the World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES), the Peritoneal Surface Oncology Group International (PSOGI), and the Italian Society of Surgical Oncology (SICO) convened a multidisciplinary working group to develop international recommendations for surgical emergencies in PSM. The project followed a staged, evidence-to-decision pathway: (i) a preliminary needs assessment; (ii) formulation of clinical questions using the PICO framework; (iii) systematic review and meta-analysis with formal grading of the certainty of evidence; (iv) drafting of statements and recommendations; (v) external review by an international expert panel; and (vi) a public consensus session.

Project steps: 2023: Preliminary survey to characterize practice patterns and perceived needs. 2024: Definition of PICO-based questions. 2025: Systematic review, meta-analysis, and GRADE assessment conducted by the Guidelines Working Team. 2025: Formulation of draft recommendations. 2025: External review by WSES, PSOGI, and SICO experts and formal consensus during the WSES Congress (Antalya, October 2025).

The key findings of the preliminary survey were: (1) marked heterogeneity in clinical practice influenced by surgical background, institutional expertise, and access to specialized care; (2) a high perceived impact of emergency management on long-term oncological outcomes—particularly emphasized by peritoneal surgeons; (3) a more proactive therapeutic stance among peritoneal surgeons compared with a generally more conservative approach among other surgeons, suggesting possible underestimation of the oncological consequences of acute decisions; and (4) strong support for guidance development, with > 90% of respondents rating dedicated guidelines as “very necessary”.

These data helped define the scope and priorities of the current guideline and guided the selection and wording of the PICO questions for the systematic review and meta-analysis. The resulting evidence base then served as the foundation for the Delphi consensus process conducted with international experts.

Methods Guideline development framework This document was developed as a consensus-based guideline in an area where high-quality direct evidence is limited. The guideline development process combined systematic evidence synthesis, formal assessment of the certainty of evidence using GRADE, and structured expert consensus. Recommendations were therefore formulated by integrating the available evidence with multidisciplinary expert judgement, clinical applicability, feasibility, and the need to support decision-making in both peripheral and referral hospitals.

Because most of the available evidence was derived from retrospective observational studies and was rated as low or very low certainty, the recommendations should be interpreted as weak, consensus-based guidance rather than strong evidence-based mandates. The statements are intended to support, not replace, individualized multidisciplinary decision-making based on clinical stability, tumor biology, expected prognosis, available expertise, patient preferences, and goals of care.

The process was coordinated by an 11-member Guidelines Working Team and involved a 23-member international expert panel from 8 countries, including experts with clinical and academic expertise in emergency surgery, surgical oncology, peritoneal surface malignancies, gastrointestinal obstruction, and evidence synthesis.

Panel selection Experts were selected according to their recognized expertise in emergency surgery, peritoneal surface malignancies, surgical oncology, gastrointestinal obstruction, and/or guideline development. Experts affiliated with WSES, PSOGI, and SICO were invited to participate in the review and consensus process. The final expert panel included 23 experts from 8 countries, with backgrounds in emergency surgery, surgical oncology, peritoneal malignancy surgery, gastrointestinal surgery, and methodology/statistics. The role of each participant, including society affiliation is reported in Supplementary Material 9 .

Statement development and consensus procedure The Guidelines Working Team formulated draft statements after completion of the systematic review, meta-analysis, risk-of-bias assessment, and GRADE evaluation. Each draft statement was based on the available evidence summary, level of evidence, strength of recommendation, and clinical applicability. Before the in-person consensus session held during the 2025 WSES Congress in Antalya, the draft statements and the results of the meta-analyses were circulated by email to the expert panel for preliminary review and written feedback. Panel members were invited to comment on the evidence summaries, indicate areas of agreement or disagreement, and suggest revisions to improve clarity, clinical applicability, and consistency with the certainty of evidence. When direct evidence specific to PSM-related malignant bowel obstruction was limited or absent, the statements were informed by indirect evidence, expert interpretation, and consensus-based clinical judgement.

Draft evidence summaries and statements were then discussed during the structured consensus session held in conjunction with the 2025 WSES Congress in Antalya, Turkey. This in-person session was used to present the evidence, discuss the clinical applicability of the draft statements, identify areas requiring clarification, and refine the wording of the recommendations. Because not all members of the international expert panel were able to attend the in-person session, the revised final document and statements were subsequently recirculated to the full expert panel for final review and voting.

Voting procedures and agreement threshold Final agreement was assessed after recirculation of the revised statements to the expert panel. Agreement was evaluated using agree/disagree vote. Consensus was predefined as agreement by at least 80% of voting participants. All final statements achieved 100% agreement among the expert panel members who completed the final voting process.

Management of disagreements Comments, requests for clarification, and disagreements raised during the in-person session or subsequent expert review were discussed by the Guidelines Working Team and incorporated into the revised statements when appropriate. Statements were reworded to improve clarity, clinical applicability, and consistency with the certainty of evidence. If the predefined consensus threshold had not been reached, the relevant statement would have been revised and submitted for further review and voting. No final statement was approved without reaching the predefined consensus threshold.

Conflict-of-interest handling All participants were asked to disclose potential conflicts of interest according to journal and society requirements. Disclosures were reviewed by the coordinating group. No conflict of interest was considered to preclude participation in the consensus process. The authors’ competing interests are reported in the Declarations section.

Society endorsement The final statements and diagnostic–therapeutic algorithm were developed through collaboration between WSES, PSOGI, and SICO experts. The final manuscript was reviewed and approved by all authors and submitted as a WSES–PSOGI–SICO consensus-based guideline. The role of each society and its representatives in the guideline development process is detailed in Supplementary Material 9 .

Review design and reporting We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA), the Cochrane Recommendations for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, and relevant Meta-analysis Of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) reporting principles (see Supplementary Material 10 ). The questions were formulated a priori according to the PICO/PIRT framework (see Supplementary Material 1 ). The working protocol, including clinical questions, eligibility criteria, outcomes, and analytic plan, was defined before study selection; the review was not prospectively registered in PROSPERO, which is acknowledged as a limitation.

Eligibility criteria Inclusion criteria Comparative studies for therapeutic PICO questions; where comparative evidence was unavailable for diagnostic or endoscopic questions, eligible non-comparative studies were retained for narrative or descriptive synthesis No age restrictions Primary and secondary peritoneal malignancies, including peritoneal metastases from colorectal, gastric, appendiceal, gynecological, pancreaticobiliary, and other cancers when reported Studies enrolling patients suffering from GI obstruction (gastric outlet, small/large bowel obstruction) in the presence of known or suspected PSM Exclusion criteria

Studies enrolling patients with GI obstruction due to primary tumor stenosis, infiltration/compression by non-peritoneal malignancies or adhesions Studies reporting overlapping series Non-English language papers Case reports, editorials, abstracts, unpublished studies, book chapters, commentaries, previously published reviews

No age restrictions were applied during study selection. However, no pediatric-specific evidence was identified, and the recommendations developed in this guideline are therefore intended primarily for adult patients. Pediatric patients with PSM-related malignant bowel obstruction should be managed through individualized multidisciplinary assessment involving pediatric surgical and oncologic expertise.

Information sources and search We searched PubMed/MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library from inception to June 2025 (English language) using PICO-specific strategies based on free-text terms for malignant bowel obstruction, peritoneal carcinomatosis/peritoneal metastases/peritoneal neoplasms, obstruction site, and the relevant diagnostic or therapeutic intervention (see Supplementary Material 1 ). Reference lists of included studies and prior reviews were also screened. The search was not extended to Embase, Scopus, or Web of Science; this source restriction is reported as a methodological limitation.

The clinical questions were formulated using the PIRT framework for the diagnostic question and the PICO framework for therapeutic questions. Specifically, PIRT was used for PICO/PIRT 1, which addressed diagnostic testing, whereas PICO was used for questions 2–5, which addressed therapeutic strategies. For simplicity, the term “PICO/PIRT questions” is used throughout the manuscript to refer to the five predefined clinical questions. Search strategies for each PIRT/PICO are reported in Supplementary Material 1 .

Study selection and data extraction After identification and removal of duplicates, two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts. Discrepancies were resolved by discussion and, when needed, by senior adjudication. Data were extracted in duplicate using standardized forms. Extracted variables included study design, country, study period, tumor origin, presence of known or suspected PSM, obstruction site, ascites or peritoneal disease burden when reported, criteria used for treatment selection, intervention and comparator details, outcome definitions, follow-up, crude event counts, effect measures, adjusted variables, and factors relevant to risk of bias.

Risk of bias and certainty of evidence Comparative non-randomized studies were assessed with ROBINS-I across seven domains (confounding; selection; classification; deviations; missing data; outcome measurement; selective reporting). Non-comparative evidence was appraised with MINORS. For the diagnostic question, no comparative diagnostic accuracy study with extractable 2 × 2 data was identified; therefore, the two CT-based retrospective series were appraised descriptively, focusing on design, population, reference standard, extractability of sensitivity/specificity, and applicability to PSM-related MBO. Certainty of evidence was graded with GRADE considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias when assessable.

Statistical analysis Odds Ratio (OR) and Mean Difference (MD) with 95% Confidence Intervals (95%CI) were selected as outcome measures for binary and continuous outcomes, respectively. Means were retrieved from each manuscript. Whenever not overtly reported, they were computed from medians, ranges, interquartile ranges (IQR), and sample sizes according to Wan’s method [ 5 ]. Meta-analyses of means and binary outcomes were developed. For non-comparative endoscopic evidence, pooled proportions or pooled means were calculated only as descriptive estimates. Common and random effects models based on Mantel–Haenszel and generic inverse variance methods, respectively, with a restricted maximum-likelihood estimator (REML) and Hartung-Knapp variance correction were developed. Between-studies heterogeneity was explored using I 2 statistic, but since it heavily depends on the precision of the included studies, τ2 and 95% prediction intervals were estimated as well. The presence of outliers was explored, and influential cases were detected through the leave-one-out method and Baujat plot. Forest plots were developed to display the results graphically. Publication bias was assessed graphically through funnel plots, and with Egger’s test only when at least 10 studies were available for an outcome, because small-study tests are unreliable and potentially misleading with fewer studies.

Software Statistical analysis was conducted with R statistical software (The Comprehensive R Archive Network – CRAN, ver. 4.4.0 × 64), using “meta”, “metafor”, “robvis”, and “dmetar”, packages. Delphi-based structured consensus process A Delphi-based structured consensus process was conducted to review, refine, and approve the final recommendations. A total of 29 experts were invited to participate in the consensus process; 23 experts from 8 countries responded and completed the final approval process.

The consensus process included two online written review rounds and one in-person consensus session held during the 2025 WSES Congress in Antalya, Turkey. During the online rounds, draft evidence summaries and preliminary statements were circulated to the expert panel. Experts were asked to provide written comments, indicate areas of agreement or disagreement, and suggest revisions regarding clinical applicability, wording, and consistency with the certainty of evidence. These online rounds were used for structured written feedback and statement refinement rather than formal voting.

Statements were modified between rounds according to expert comments, requests for clarification, and concerns regarding clinical applicability and evidence alignment. All experts were invited to comment on all statements. During the in-person consensus session in Antalya, the revised statements were presented and discussed. Formal voting was performed using an “agree/not agree” format. Consensus was predefined as agreement by at least 80% of voting participants. Voting was not anonymous.

Because not all members of the international expert panel were able to attend the in-person session, the revised final document and statements were subsequently recirculated to all 23 responding expert panel members for final review and confirmation. All final statements achieved 100% agreement among the 23 expert panel members who completed the final approval process.

Comments, disagreements, or requests for clarification raised during the online review rounds, the in-person session, or the final recirculation were addressed by the Guidelines Working Team and incorporated into revised statements when appropriate. If the predefined consensus threshold had not been reached, the relevant statement would have been further revised and resubmitted for additional review and voting. No final statement was approved without reaching the predefined consensus threshold.

Evidence basis of recommendations For each statement, the evidence basis was explicitly reviewed to distinguish recommendations supported by direct evidence from studies including patients with malignant bowel obstruction due to peritoneal carcinomatosis/peritoneal surface malignancies from operational notes informed by indirect evidence or expert consensus. Statements 2–5 were based on evidence retrieved from studies specifically including patients with obstruction in the context of PSM. Statement 1 was based on the limited available direct evidence on CT in this population, together with expert interpretation of its clinical applicability.

When indirect evidence was used for practical management notes, this was explicitly labelled. In particular, the water-soluble contrast challenge was included as an operational note extrapolated from guidelines for adhesive small-bowel obstruction and was not used to upgrade the level of evidence or strength of recommendation.

Results Overview of previous systematic reviews Seven prior systematic reviews or consensus-based reviews were identified [ 6 – 12 ] (see Supplementary Material 2 ); AMSTAR appraisal judged most to be of very low methodological quality, except one moderate-quality review [ 6 ]. Additional topic-specific reviews identified in the supplementary evidence tables were used to contextualize specific questions when relevant. Systematic review and meta-analysis The present review included retrospective observational studies only; no randomized trials were identified. Supplementary Material 3 reports the characteristics of included studies and the excluded studies with reasons.

PIRT 1 – DIAGNOSIS Should patients with MBO and PSM receive abdominal CT, abdominal x-ray or abdominal x-ray with gastrografin for diagnosis? Key outcomes Sensitivity, Specificity for the diagnosis of bowel obstruction due to PSM. Current evidence summary No studies have assessed the diagnostic performance of plain abdominal X-ray, Gastrografin-enhanced abdominal X-ray specifically in patients with MBO due to PSM (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 PRISMA for PICO 1

Only two small retrospective CT-based studies were identified in this population (Fig. 2 ). They were judged to provide very low-certainty evidence because they were non-comparative or indirectly comparative, had small sample sizes, heterogeneous populations and target conditions, and did not provide sufficiently comparable 2 × 2 diagnostic accuracy data for the index tests specified in the PIRT. Therefore, a diagnostic meta-analysis was not performed. The decision not to pool was based on non-comparability of outcomes and extractable effect measures rather than on the number of studies alone. Fig. 2 PRISMA for proportion meta-analysis

Methodological appraisal of the two CT-based studies: Ha et al. [ 13 ] evaluated CT in postoperative obstruction after surgery for malignancy and reported reader accuracy and a multivariable model for malignant versus benign causes, but the population was not restricted to PSM and the reference standard was not uniform for all patients. Miccò et al. [ 14 ] described prognostic CT findings in ovarian cancer-related MBO, but did not compare CT with abdominal X-ray or Gastrografin-enhanced X-ray and did not report extractable sensitivity/specificity for diagnosis of PSM-related obstruction. These limitations justify narrative synthesis and a very low certainty rating.

Ha et al. [ 13 ] retrospectively evaluated 55 patients with postoperative intestinal obstruction after abdominal surgery for malignancy (29 malignant, 26 benign). All patients underwent an abdominal CT scan with intravenous contrast, and among them, 25 also received oral contrast. Diagnostic accuracies of three independent readers for differentiating malignant from benign causes of bowel obstruction were 67%, 75%, and 78%. Using a multivariable model restricted to two CT features (a mass at the obstructed or prior surgical site and lymphadenopathy), the overall diagnostic accuracy was 84% (46/55), with a positive predictive value of 92% for malignant obstruction and a negative predictive value of 77%. CT findings favoring malignancy included an abrupt transition zone and irregular bowel wall thickening at the obstructed site; features favoring benign obstruction included a smooth transition zone, smooth wall thickening, and a larger amount of ascites.

Miccò et al. [ 14 ] included 31 women with advanced ovarian cancer and MBO. All patients received nonionic intravenous contrast material. Bowel wall thinning ( p = 0.03), mesenteric tumor deposits ( p = 0.009), mesenteric infiltration ( p = 0.02), and ascites ( p = 0.04) were associated with shorter survival; ROC analysis reported an AUC of 0.728 ( p = 0.03) for mesenteric tumor deposits as a predictor in this setting. Median overall survival in this cohort was 90 days.

In summary, CT provides actionable diagnostic information in this population (particularly for differentiating malignant vs benign causes and mapping obstruction sites), but comparative accuracy versus plain X‑ray or Gastrografin studies has not been established; the evidence base is limited to small, retrospective series. Level of evidence (LoE) Very low (two retrospective, non-comparative studies with small sample size). Strength of recommendation (SoR) Weak - recommendation based on limited, non-comparative evidence.

Key discussion points raised by the expert panel Beyond the low-certainty evidence, the panel agreed on two consensus-derived points. First, there is no specific evidence supporting routine oral contrast for the diagnosis of MBO in this population and its use should not delay urgent decision-making. Second, the role of contrast-enhanced CT established for adhesive small-bowel obstruction [ 15 ] can be reasonably extended to MBO due to PSM to define transition points and rule out “never-miss” complications; however, this extrapolation does not warrant upgrading the strength of recommendation at this stage. Statement 1

In patients with suspected MBO due to PSM, CT with intravenous contrast allows differentiation between benign and malignant causes of obstruction, provides localization of single or multiple obstruction sites, and identifies urgent surgical conditions such as perforation, ischemia, or volvulus. Therefore, we suggest that CT with intravenous contrast may be considered the initial cross-sectional imaging modality to support clinical decision-making in this patient population. [LoE: Very Low; SoR: Weak in favor] . [Level of agreement: 100% agreement among the expert panel members who completed the final voting process after recirculation of the revised document.]

PICO 2-Type of treatment Should patients with MBO and PSM receive an attempt at medical therapy (including nasogastric tube, NPT, hydration, gastrografin, antiemetics, somatostatin) or surgical/endoscopic therapy? Key outcomes Clinical Success rate (defined as the clinical resolution of bowel obstruction), mortality, morbidity, length of stay (LOS), overall survival (OS), re-obstruction rate.

Previous systematic review and meta-analyses The available reviews related to this PICO [ 6 – 8 , 10 , 11 ] (See Supplementary Material 2 ) reported heterogeneous findings. Olson [ 7 ], Idaikkadar [ 11 ], Toth [ 10 ], Bansal [ 8 ] were judged to be of very low methodological quality according to AMSTAR. The review by Kukukmentin [ 6 ] was rated as moderate quality. However, this review included only a single retrospective study [ 16 ], limiting its overall impact. The study analysed retrospective data for 47 women who received either palliative surgery or medical management with Octreotide and reported overall survival and perioperative mortality and morbidity. Multivariable analysis found that women who received surgery had significantly better survival than those treated with Octreotide, after adjustment for important prognostic factors. More recent reviews and the Delphi consensus [ 8 ] emphasized the role of nonoperative medical management as initial therapy, reserving surgery for highly selected cases. The overall quality of evidence remains low, with significant risk of bias and heterogeneity across studies.

Current evidence summary The evidence regarding the management of MBO in patients with PSM derives from a limited number of retrospective observational studies [ 16 – 24 ] (Fig. 3 , Table 1 ) with meta-analyses available for binary and continuous outcomes. Success rate Results Four studies [ 16 – 19 ], including a total of 206 patients, compared medical and surgical/endoscopic interventions in terms of treatment success (Fig. 4 ). Pooled results did not demonstrate a significant difference between the two strategies (Random-effects model – OR 0.54, 95% CI: 0.11–2.58 – p = 0.3), although heterogeneity was moderate (I 2 = 45.2%; τ 2 = 0.43) and there was uncertainty in external validity (prediction interval (PI) = 0.016–18.51). No outliers or influential cases were detected; therefore, no sensitivity analysis was performed. This indicates that medical therapy may achieve comparable rates of initial symptom control to surgery or endoscopic procedures, albeit with substantial uncertainty due to limited sample size and variability across studies. Fig. 4 PICO 2: Forest plot for success rate

Risk of bias The overall risk of bias across the four included studies was judged as serious (see Supplementary Material 5 ). The main concerns were related to confounding, with several studies rated at serious risk in these domains. Selection of participants, deviations from intended interventions and missing data were generally judged at moderate risk. These limitations highlight the fragility of the available evidence and should be considered when interpreting the results of the meta-analysis. Assessment of publication bias was not feasible given the limited number of included studies (< 10).

Morbidity Results Three studies [ 16 – 18 ], with 158 patients, reported postoperative or treatment-related morbidity (Fig. 5 ). Morbidity was study-defined and included postoperative complications and procedure- or treatment-related adverse events; definitions varied across studies and were not consistently graded, limiting clinical granularity. Medical therapy was associated with a lower risk of complications compared with surgery (random-effects model: OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07-0.39; p = 0.012). Heterogeneity was negligible (I 2 = 0%), suggesting statistical consistency, although the prediction interval remained wide (PI = 0.012–2.14). No outliers or influential cases were detected; therefore, no sensitivity analysis was performed. These results suggest that interventional treatment carries a higher complication burden in this frail patient population, but the non-standardized morbidity definitions require cautious interpretation. Fig. 5 PICO 2: Forest plot for morbidity

RoB The overall risk of bias for the three studies reporting morbidity was judged as serious (see Supplementary Material 5 ). The main concerns were related to confounding, with several studies rated at serious risk in these domains. Selection of participants, deviations from intended interventions and missing data were frequently assessed as at moderate risk. Overall, these limitations reduce the confidence in the effect estimates for morbidity and indicate that the evidence should be interpreted with caution. Assessment of publication bias was not feasible given the limited number of included studies (< 10).

Mortality Results Three studies [ 16 , 18 , 19 ], with 354344 patients, reported postoperative or treatment-related mortality. Two separate meta-analyses were performed for mortality, depending on the comparator group of Sun [ 20 ].

The main analysis (Fig. 6 a) included 3 studies with Sun [ 20 ] having endoscopy as comparator. This analysis showed no significant differences between medical and endoscopic therapy (Random-effects model – OR 2.27 (95% CI: 0-23196 – p = 0.74)) with extreme heterogeneity (I2=96%, τ 2 = 12.7) and high uncertainty in external validity (PI = 0–2.06 × 10 23 ), yielding non-significant results. Fig. 6 a PICO 2: Forest plot for mortality with Sun [ 20 ] having endoscopy as comparator b PICO 2: Forest plot for mortality with Sun [ 20 ] having surgery as comparator

A sensitivity analysis (Fig. 6 b) included the same 3 studies with Sun [ 20 ] having surgery as comparator. Also in this case, no significant differences were observed between medical and surgical therapy (Random-effects model – OR 4.47 (95% CI: 0.007-2697 – p = 0.42)), again with very high heterogeneity (I2=85%, τ 2 = 5.28) and high uncertainty in external validity (PI = 0-5.69 × 10 15 ). Both analyses were strongly influenced by large datasets (particularly Sun [ 20 ] and Mangili [ 16 ]), and sensitivity analyses were not performed because after excluding these studies left insufficient data to draw reliable conclusions.

The prediction interval spanned from near-zero to astronomically large harm, indicating that the effect is highly inconsistent across studies. The evidence base is too heterogeneous and unbalanced to draw reliable conclusions. The evidence is dominated by one very large study [ 20 ], with influence analysis confirming disproportionate weight, which limits the reliability of the pooled estimate. Overall, the evidence on mortality is inconsistent and does not allow robust comparisons between medical and surgical strategies.

RoB Across the studies reporting mortality, the overall risk of bias is serious (see Supplementary Material 4 ). The domain most frequently at high concern is confounding: two key studies are rated serious risk here, driving the overall judgement. Deviations from intended interventions, missing data and selection of the reported result are commonly moderate risk. At the study level, the largest datasets carry serious overall risk (due to residual confounding). These limitations—particularly the serious risk of confounding in the most influential studies—substantially reduce confidence in the pooled mortality estimates and help explain the inconsistency and imprecision observed.

Length of stay (LOS) Results Length of hospital stay was reported in four studies [ 17 – 20 ]. Two distinct meta-analyses were performed for hospital LOS according to the comparator in Sun [ 20 ] (Fig. 7 ). Fig. 7 a PICO 2: Forest plot for length of stay with Sun [ 20 ] having endoscopy as comparator; b Forest plot for length of stay with Sun [ 20 ] having endoscopy as comparator after sensitivity analysis; c Forest plot for length of stay with Sun [ 20 ] having surgery as comparator

The first analysis, including 4 studies with Sun [ 20 ] having endoscopy as comparator, demonstrated significantly shorter hospitalization in the medical group (Random-effects model–MD − 9.48, 95% CI: − 12.65– − 6.32 – p = 0.0024). Heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 52%, τ 2 = 2.99), largely driven by Sun [ 20 ], and there was consistent benefit in external validity (PI = − 18.07– − 0.9). No outliers were detected. Sun [ 20 ] was detected as an influential case.

Sensitivity analysis excluding this study confirmed the advantage of medical management, with a reduction of approximately 11 days (Random-effects model–MD − 11.16, 95% CI: − 11.66– − 10.65 – p = 0.0001), no residual heterogeneity (I2 = 0.0%, τ 2 = 0) and consistent benefit in external validity (PI = − 12.63– − 9.68).

The second analysis, including 4 studies with Sun [ 20 ] having surgery as comparator, consistently showed a reduction of about 10 days in favor of medical therapy (Random-effects model–MD − 10.41, 95% CI: − 10.55– − 10.27 – p < 0.001), with no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%, τ2 = 0) and consistent benefit in external validity (PI = − 10.6– − 10.22). No outliers or influential cases were detected.

These findings provide robust evidence that noninterventional treatment is associated with substantially shorter hospital stays compared with both surgical and endoscopic interventions, with a mean reduction of 8–11 days. This difference remained consistent across sensitivity analyses, even after exclusion of large influential datasets (e.g. Sun [ 20 ]). These findings underscore the lower burden of hospitalization associated with nonoperative therapy, an important consideration for patients with limited life expectancy.

RoB For the outcome length of hospital stay, the included studies were judged at serious overall risk of bias (see Supplementary Material 4 ). The main concerns were confounding, selective reporting, missing data and deviations from intended interventions, which were rated at moderate risk across all studies.

After sensitivity analysis, the overall risk of bias for LOS was very serious (see Supplementary Material 4 ). The main concerns were confounding, consistently rated at serious risk, and selective reporting and deviations from intended interventions, which were judged as moderate across all studies. In summary, although sensitivity analysis improved the statistical consistency of the LOS results, the certainty of evidence was more limited by the serious risk of bias in key domains. Publication bias not assessed due to the limited number of studies.

Re-obstruction rate We considered the re-obstruction rate as a relevant outcome to assess treatment effectiveness; however, the available data are limited. Only two studies, Akbas et al. [ 17 ] and Woolfson et al. [ 19 ], reported the re-obstruction rate : 60.7% (17/28) in the medical treatment group and 33.3% (16/48) in the surgical group in Akbas [ 17 ], and 18.8% (3/16) vs 12.5% (4/32) in Woolfson [ 19 ]. Bryan et al. [ 18 ] instead reported re-obstruction-free survival , with a mean of 6.4 ± 6 months for medical treatment and 5.1 ± 10 months for surgical treatment. Overall, the paucity and heterogeneity of the data do not allow for a meta-analysis on this outcome.

Overall risk of bias When considering all outcomes together, the overall risk of bias across the included studies was judged as serious (see Supplementary Material 4 ). The most recurrent limitation was confounding, with several studies—particularly large retrospective cohorts—rated at serious risk due to lack of adjustment for important prognostic factors. In addition, selective reporting was consistently judged at moderate risk, reflecting incomplete reporting. Other domains were less problematic: selection of participants, classification of interventions, and measurement of outcomes were mostly low risk, while deviations from intended interventions and missing data were more often assessed as moderate.

Level of evidence (LoE) According to the GRADE evaluation, the certainty of evidence for this PICO is overall low to very low , with the exception of length of hospital stay (see Supplementary Material 5 ). Success rate: Very low certainty – Four non-randomised studies, with serious risk of bias and inconsistency. The confidence and prediction intervals were extremely wide, including both potential benefit and harm. Morbidity: Low certainty – Three studies suggested lower morbidity with medical therapy (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07–0.39), but two out of three had serious risk of bias and the prediction interval included the possibility of no effect.

Mortality: Very low certainty – Three studies showed extremely heterogeneous and imprecise results, with confidence intervals spanning from negligible to very large effects; the random-effects estimate was uninformative. Length of hospital stay (LOS) : Moderate certainty – Four studies showed consistently shorter LOS with medical therapy (MD –9.48 days, 95% CI − 12.65 to − 6.32). However, after sensitivity analysis excluding outliers, certainty decreased to low (MD − 11.16 days, 95% CI − 11.66 to − 10.65) because all remaining studies were at serious risk of bias.

In summary: the most consistent evidence supports medical therapy as being associated with fewer complications and shorter hospital stay, although even these outcomes are limited by study quality. For success rate and mortality, the certainty of evidence is very low, and no firm conclusions can be drawn. Strength of recommendation (SoR) Weak.

Key discussion points raised by the expert panel Where direct comparative data are sparse, the panel endorsed operational rules to standardize nonoperative care. The Gastrografin challenge—as used in adhesive SBO [ 15 ] —can be reasonably extended to PSM-related MBO to accelerate decisions. Nonoperative management should be time-boxed to 72 h with explicit failure criteria (persistent obstruction > 72 h; NGT output > 500 mL on day 3; clinical deterioration such as peritonitis or ischemia).

The panel also discussed the role of corticosteroids as part of symptomatic nonoperative management. Corticosteroids were not intentionally excluded from the therapeutic approach; however, no PSM-specific comparative studies allowed assessment of their independent effect on obstruction resolution, morbidity, mortality, length of stay, re-obstruction, or overall survival. In the available literature, medical management was usually reported as a heterogeneous bundle of interventions, making it impossible to isolate corticosteroid-specific outcomes. Therefore, corticosteroids were considered a potential component of individualized medical therapy, rather than a separately graded intervention.

The acute episode should be managed in any capable hospital (peripheral or HUB) , with referral to specialized PSM centers after stabilization, aligning with the aim of these guidelines to harmonize care across settings. The panel also noted likely selection bias across treatment groups and the absence of validated scores and studies focused on the quality of life specific to this population for life expectancy or performance status. Finally, no absolute contraindications to surgery were identified beyond patient refusal and futility of care in terminal patients. Statement 2

In patients with MBO due to PSM, and in the absence of urgent surgical indications (perforation, ischemia, shock), we suggest an initial attempt at nonoperative medical management, as it seems to be feasible and not associated with an increased risk of complications. When successful in resolving the obstruction, it may result in a shorter hospital stay. [LoE: Low/Very low, SoR: Weak in favor] [Level of agreement: 100% agreement among the expert panel members who completed the final voting process after recirculation of the revised document.] Notes on the recommendation Definition of nonoperative management.

Nonoperative management includes nil per os , IV fluid resuscitation, and nasogastric tube (NGT) decompression. Use of a water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) challenge. In patients selected for a trial of nonoperative therapy, a Gastrografin challenge can be used to guide management. If contrast is visualized in the colon within 24–36 h, continue nonoperative treatment ; if not, surgical intervention should be considered. Definition of failure of nonoperative therapy. Escalation to operative or alternative interventions should be considered in the following situations: Persistent obstruction > 72 h despite optimal nonoperative measures; NGT drainage volume > 500 mL on day 3;

Clinical deterioration suggestive of peritonitis or intestinal ischemia. Contraindications to surgery. Surgery is contraindicated when the patient refuses operative management or when care is deemed futile in terminal patients . Post-episode disposition. After resolution of the acute episode, patients should be referred—or at least considered for referral—to a specialized PSM center for multidisciplinary evaluation and ongoing care. Evidence. The available evidence regarding success rates , overall survival , and mortality with nonoperative management in PSM-related MBO remains inconclusive .

PICO 3-Type of treatment Should patients with MBO and PSM receive surgical therapy or endoscopic treatment (including stenting, Endoscopic US-guided bypass with lumen apposing metal stent—LAMS)? Key outcomes Clinical Success rate (defined as the clinical resolution of bowel obstruction), mortality, morbidity, length of stay (LOS), overall survival (OS).

Previous systematic review and meta-analyses Previous systematic reviews, including Olson [ 7 ], Toth [ 9 ], and Bansal [ 8 ], all judged to be of very low methodological quality according to AMSTAR (See Supplementary Material 2 ), highlighted the lack of high-quality comparative evidence between surgical and endoscopic approaches. Olson [ 7 ] suggested that surgery often achieves higher palliation rates but carries higher risks of morbidity and mortality. Toth [ 10 ] reported heterogeneous results with no clear superiority of one approach, emphasizing the importance of patient selection. The Delphi consensus (Bansal [ 8 ]) stressed the need for prospective trials, given the overall low level of evidence and methodological limitations of the available studies.

Current evidence summary The evidence comparing surgical and endoscopic management of malignant bowel obstruction in patients with peritoneal carcinomatosis derives from a small number of observational studies [ 20 , 27 – 31 ] (Fig. 8 , Table 2 ), with meta-analyses available for binary and continuous outcomes. The evidence for PICO 3 is heterogeneous and largely limited by non-randomized designs and confounding. Surgery may offer higher success, while endoscopy is associated with shorter LOS, without difference in mortality rate. Certainty of evidence remains low/very low for most outcomes, with only LOS reaching moderate certainty. Strength of recommendation (SoR) Weak. Statement 3

3.1 We suggest considering a surgical approach in patients with MBO due to PSM who have good performance status and reasonable life expectancy, after failure of nonoperative medical management. In selected observational cohorts, surgery seems to be associated with higher success rates than endoscopic treatment, while available data did not show an increase in short-term mortality. [LoE: Low. SoR: Weak in favor]

3.2 We suggest endoscopic treatment as a palliative option, in patients with poor performance status or limited life expectancy, after failure of nonoperative medical management and when the obstruction is technically amenable to endoscopic palliation. PICO 4-Type of treatment Should patients with malignant bowel obstruction (MBO) and peritoneal surface malignancies (PSM) who are candidates for surgical therapy receive bowel resection, stoma, or bypass? Key outcomes Mortality, morbidity, OS, LOS, Clinical Success rate (defined as the clinical resolution of bowel obstruction).

Previous systematic reviews or meta-analyses The systematic review by Shariat-Madar [ 9 ], judged to be of very low methodological quality according to AMSTAR (See Supplementary Material 2 ), synthesized 5 studies, reporting that resection achieved longer survival (median 7.2 months) compared with bypass (2.7 months) or ostomy (3.4 months), but with a higher rate of complications. The review concluded that resection may provide survival benefit in selected patients, although the evidence was limited and at risk of bias.

Current evidence summary The evidence comparing bowel resection, ostomy and bypass in patients with malignant bowel obstruction due to peritoneal carcinomatosis derives from a small number of observational studies [ 31 – 35 ], with meta-analyses available for binary and continuous outcomes (Fig. 13 , Table 3 ). Three studies (101 patients) [ 31 – 33 ] compared morbidity between resection and bypass. No significant differences emerged (Random-effects model–OR 1.27, 95% CI: 0.46–3.52 – p = 0.41), with no heterogeneity (I 2 = 0%; τ 2 = 0), but uncertainty in external validity (PI = 0.06–25.57). No outliers were detected, nor influential cases (Fig. 15 b). Overall, perioperative complication rates appear similar between resection and diversion/bypass procedures.

RoB For the studies included, the overall risk of bias was judged as very serious (see Supplementary Material 4 ). The most relevant limitation was confounding, rated as serious in all studies, due to the retrospective, non-randomized design and lack of adequate adjustment for prognostic factors. LOS None of the included studies reported comparative data on the length of hospital stay for patients undergoing resection, bypass, or ostomy.

Overall risk of bias For PICO 4, the overall risk of bias was judged as very serious (see Supplementary Material 4 ). The predominant limitation across all included studies was confounding, systematically rated as serious due to the retrospective design and lack of appropriate adjustment for clinical and prognostic factors.

Other domains, such as selection of participants, classification of interventions, missing data and measurement of outcomes, were mostly at low risk, suggesting adequate methodological conduct in these aspects. However, deviations from intended interventions and selective reporting were frequently rated as moderate risk, reflecting incomplete data reporting and possible outcome selection. Level of evidence (LoE) According to the GRADE evaluation, the certainty of evidence for this PICO is very low across all reported outcomes. (see Supplementary Material 7 ).

Mortality: Very low certainty – Three retrospective studies (n = 98) suggest that bowel resection is associated with higher mortality compared with stoma or bypass (OR 3.55, 95% CI 1.45–8.68). However, all studies were judged at serious risk of bias, and imprecision was very high due to wide confidence and prediction intervals, which included both minimal effect and very large harm.

Morbidity: Very low certainty – Three studies (n = 101) reported no significant difference in morbidity between resection and bypass/ostomy (OR 1.27, 95% CI 0.46–3.52). All were at serious risk of bias, with very wide confidence and prediction intervals [0.06–25.57], reflecting small sample sizes and substantial imprecision. Other outcomes (success rate, OS, LOS): Not enough studies reported these outcomes to allow a meta-analysis. Available evidence was scarce, fragmented, and inconsistent, preventing any conclusions.

The evidence base for PICO 4 is limited to very small, retrospective studies, all at very serious risk of bias. Mortality appears higher with resection, but the certainty of evidence is very low, as is the certainty for morbidity. No conclusions can be drawn for success rate, overall survival, or LOS. Strength of recommendation (SoR) Weak. Statement 4

In patients with MBO due to PSM who require urgent surgical intervention (and are not in the terminal phase of disease), as well as in patients undergoing urgent surgery for bowel obstruction in whom peritoneal disease is unexpectedly found, we suggest preferring bypass or ostomy over resection, when technically feasible, given a signal toward lower perioperative mortality. [ LoE: Very low, SoR: Weak ] [Level of agreement: 100% agreement among the expert panel members who completed the final voting process after recirculation of the revised document.] Notes on the recommendation

Evidence on morbidity is uncertain, and data on success rate, overall survival, and length of stay are insufficient. After the acute episode, patients should be considered for referral to a specialized peritoneal surface malignancies center. PICO 5-Type of treatment Should patients with MBO and PSM candidates for endoscopic therapy receive endoscopic stenting or Endoscopic US-guided bypass with lumen apposing metal stent (LAMS)? Key outcomes Mortality, morbidity, OS, LOS, Clinical Success rate (defined as the clinical resolution of bowel obstruction). Previous systematic reviews or meta-analyses No prior review or meta-analyses specifically addressed this population.

Current evidence summary There are no comparative studies directly evaluating endoscopic stenting versus endoscopic ultrasound-guided bypass with lumen-apposing metal stents (LAMS) in patients with malignant bowel obstruction (MBO) due to PSM (Fig. 16 ). Therefore, only descriptive meta-analyses of mean/proportion are available. Consequently, it is not possible to directly answer the original PICO question. For this reason, the question was reformulated as: ‘Is it safe and effective for patients with MBO and PSM eligible for endoscopic therapy to receive endoscopic stenting or endoscopic US-guided bypass with lumen-apposing metal stents (LAMS)?’ and a descriptive meta-analysis was performed (Fig. 17 , Table 4 ). LAMS Evidence on LAMS in this specific population is limited to a single retrospective study by Abbas et al. [ 27 ], which included 37 patients with malignant gastric outlet obstruction treated with EUS-guided gastrojejunostomy using LAMS. The technical success rate was 92%, while clinical success was achieved in 81% of cases. Median overall survival was 98 days, with a 30-day mortality of 8%. Post-procedural adverse events occurred in 11% of patients, mostly mild to moderate in severity.

Endoscopic stenting The evidence reporting outcomes of endoscopic stenting in patients with malignant bowel obstruction due to peritoneal carcinomatosis derives from some observational studies [ 23 , 28 – 31 , 36 – 41 ], with mean/proportion meta-analyses available for binary and continuous outcomes.

Success rate Results A meta-analysis of 10 studies [ 23 , 28 , 29 , 31 , 36 – 43 ] including 650 patients reported a pooled success rate under random-effects model of 0.71 (95% CI: 0.62–0.79) (0.79 for gastric outlet obstruction and 0.66 for large bowel obstruction), moderate heterogeneity (I 2 = 66.4; τ 2 = 0.19) and uncertainty in external validity (PI = 0.46–0.87) (Fig. 18 a). Fig. 18 a PICO 5-Forest plot for success rate; b PICO 5-Forest plot for success rate after sensitivity analysis

Sensitivity analysis (after removal of Kim [ 28 ]) pointed out a pooled success rate of 0.74 (95%CI: 0.66–0.8) (0.79 for gastric outlet obstruction and 0.69 for large bowel obstruction), low-to-moderate heterogeneity (I 2 = 39.7; τ 2 = 0.07) and uncertainty in external validity (PI = 0.58–0.85) (Fig. 18 b). Most of the uncertainty in external validity arises from the subgroup gastric outlet obstruction. For patients belonging to the “large bowel” subgroup the results are more stable and robust. Assessment of publication bias with Egger’s test did not show evidence of bias (see Supplementary Material 4 ).

Morbidity Results Morbidity was reported in 7 studies (341 patients) [ 23 , 28 , 29 , 36 , 40 , 42 , 43 ]. Reported events included adverse events after endoscopic stenting or related procedures, including perforation, migration or occlusion where reported, bleeding, infection, and other study-defined complications. The pooled morbidity rate under a random-effects model was 0.17 (95% CI 0.06–0.38), with high heterogeneity (I 2 = 84.3%; τ2 = 1.17) and substantial uncertainty in external validity (PI = 0.01–0.81) (Fig. 19 a). Sensitivity analysis after removal of Mendelsohn [ 40 ] and Choi [ 36 ] showed a pooled morbidity of 0.18 (95% CI 0.09–0.32), moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 48.9%; τ2 = 0.27), and persistent uncertainty (PI = 0.03–0.59) (Fig. 19 b). Using ROBINS-I, the main concern was confounding, consistently rated as moderate to serious due to the retrospective and observational nature of all included studies, with insufficient adjustment for prognostic variables. Other domains—such as selection of participants, classification of interventions and missing data—were generally rated as low to moderate risk, with some variability across studies. Reporting bias and deviations from intended interventions were also a recurrent issue, given incomplete outcome reporting.

According to the MINORS tool (for non-comparative studies), most domains were rated at low risk, but statistical analysis and data collection showed recurrent serious limitations, reflecting incomplete methodological transparency and heterogeneity in data quality across studies. In summary, the evidence for PICO 5 is largely based on small, retrospective observational studies. The predominance of confounding, incomplete data collection, and limited statistical robustness leads to an overall serious risk of bias.

Level of evidence (LoE) According to the GRADE evaluation, the certainty of evidence for this PICO is very low across all reported outcomes. The available evidence on endoscopic stenting for malignant bowel obstruction in patients with peritoneal carcinomatosis is of very low certainty, being based on small, retrospective studies with serious risk of bias. Endoscopic stenting shows a good clinical success rate and low early mortality, but outcomes are highly variable. Data on LAMS are currently limited to a single retrospective study (see Supplementary Material 8 ). Strength of recommendation (SoR) Weak.

Key discussion points raised by the expert panel The panel discussed how best to manage patients who remain candidates for biological or targeted therapies. Given the current evidence base and the need to preserve oncologic options, the consensus position is to restrict endoscopic palliation to patients receiving palliative care, whereas patients with ongoing disease-modifying trajectories should preferentially undergo strategies that maintain eligibility for systemic treatments. Statement 5

In patients with large bowel obstruction or gastric outlet obstruction due to PSM who fail nonoperative medical therapy and are not candidates for surgery (because of poor performance status, or limited life expectancy), we suggest endoscopic stent placement as a valid option in the palliative setting. [LoE: Very low, SoR: Weak in favor] [Level of agreement: 100% agreement among the expert panel members who completed the final voting process after recirculation of the revised document.] Notes on the recommendation

Descriptive evidence suggests that endoscopic stenting may achieve acceptable clinical success and low early mortality in selected patients, especially in large bowel obstruction, but the evidence is highly heterogeneous and of very low certainty. Data on LAMS are currently limited to a single retrospective study focusing on gastric outlet obstruction, and further comparative trials are needed. After the acute episode, if appropriate, patients should be referred to a specialized PSM center.

The algorithm should not be interpreted as a standalone decision rule, but as an operational synthesis of the five consensus-based statements. The algorithm is derived from Statements 1–5 and should be interpreted together with the corresponding LoE, SoR, evidence basis, and practical notes reported in Table 5 Discussion Principal findings This manuscript should be interpreted as a consensus-based guideline rather than as a set of strong evidence-based recommendations, because the available evidence remains largely retrospective, heterogeneous, and of low or very low certainty.

However, this systematic review and meta-analysis, integrated with a formal Delphi process and consensus among international experts from WSES, PSOGI, and SICO, provides the first structured, international recommendations for emergency management of patients with peritoneal surface malignancies (PSM). Although the certainty of evidence is mostly low to very low and based on retrospective cohorts, several clinically relevant signals emerged. Contrast-enhanced CT may provide useful information to map obstruction sites and identify urgent surgical conditions, but direct comparative evidence against plain abdominal X-ray or Gastrografin studies in PSM-related MBO remains lacking. An initial trial of nonoperative medical management appears feasible in the absence of urgent surgical indications and may be associated with shorter hospitalization when successful, although the evidence remains limited by confounding and heterogeneity. After failure of nonoperative therapy, surgery may be considered in carefully selected patients with good performance status and reasonable life expectancy, whereas endoscopic approaches may reduce hospitalization burden in patients with limited prognosis or poor performance status. In patients requiring urgent surgery, diversion or bypass may be favored over resection when technically feasible, given a signal toward lower perioperative mortality.

Because the certainty of evidence was low or very low for most outcomes, all recommendations should be interpreted as weak, consensus-based guidance rather than strong evidence-based mandates. The proposed statements are intended to support, not replace, individualized multidisciplinary decision-making, taking into account clinical stability, tumor biology, expected prognosis, available expertise, patient preferences, and goals of care.

Interpretation and clinical implications Patients with PSM presenting with MBO were historically considered incurable and they are often considered as patients with uniformly poor prognosis and predominantly symptom-directed care. Contemporary oncologic strategies—including cytoreductive surgery (CRS) and modern systemic or intraperitoneal therapies—have reshaped this paradigm: in carefully selected patients, durable disease control and even long-term survival are attainable. Consequently, what happens during the emergency episode matters: early, structured decision-making can preserve options for downstream oncologic treatments and influence overall prognosis. Furthermore, in patients who underwent palliative surgery and had symptoms resolution or re-established gastrointestinal function, the access to systemic chemotherapy after surgery is the only factor related to survival [ 44 ].

Care pathways and referral Beyond the index admission, early linkage to specialized PSM centers enables multidisciplinary reassessment, formal staging, and timely access to disease-modifying therapies when appropriate. However, referral pathways must be adapted to the urgency and stability of the clinical scenario.

In clinically unstable patients, or in the presence of perforation, peritonitis, ischemia, shock, or other “never-miss” surgical conditions, immediate local emergency management should not be delayed by transfer. In these situations, the priority is source control, resuscitation, and management of the acute surgical condition in the hospital where the patient presents, provided that appropriate emergency surgical expertise is available.

In clinically stable patients without immediate surgical indications, early discussion with a specialized PSM center may help guide treatment selection, define whether transfer is appropriate, and preserve future oncologic options. Similarly, after resolution or stabilization of the acute episode, patients should be referred to, or at least discussed with, a specialized PSM center for multidisciplinary reassessment and planning of further oncologic or surgical management.

When consultation with a PSM referral center is requested, the minimum information to be shared should include: primary tumor type and oncologic history; previous abdominal surgery, CRS, or HIPEC; current and planned systemic or locoregional treatment options; performance status; nutritional status; patient goals of care; CT findings, including obstruction site or sites, presence of ascites, extent of peritoneal disease, suspected peritoneal cancer index when available, distant metastases; intraoperative findings if surgery has already been performed, including the extent and distribution of peritoneal disease (Peritoneal Cancer Index if available), feasibility of complete cytoreduction if assessable, and any performed procedure; laboratory abnormalities; and the response to initial nonoperative management.

Quality of life and patient-reported outcomes: the missing piece Across the included studies, outcomes were largely limited to technical success, complications, length of stay, and crude survival, with scarce and heterogeneous reporting of quality of life or other patient-reported outcomes (PRO). However, this outcome is very difficult to assess in so frail and compromised patients and no validated PRO measures are available in the current literature. This gap is particularly consequential in PSM-related MBO, where decisions often balance short-term symptom relief, procedure-related burden (e.g., stomas, tubes, re-admissions), and preservation of eligibility for disease-modifying therapies. The absence of standardized PRO measures, baseline assessments, longitudinal follow-up, and predefined minimally important differences undermines the interpretability and patient-centeredness of the current evidence. Consequently, treatments that appear similar when judged solely by traditional clinical endpoints may, in reality, have very different impacts on a patient’s daily life. Some therapies may offer better relief of troublesome symptoms, help patients preserve independence and functional ability, allow them to spend more meaningful time at home rather than in the hospital, and reduce the physical and emotional strain placed on caregivers. These aspects—often overlooked in conventional outcome measures—are especially important to patients facing a limited prognosis, for whom quality of life and time spent with loved ones are paramount. Future research should incorporate a core outcome set that includes validated PRO instruments.

Limitations Several limitations must be explicitly acknowledged. First, the search was limited to PubMed/MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library and to English-language studies; Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were not searched. This may have reduced retrieval sensitivity and should be considered when interpreting the evidence base. Second, all included primary studies were observational and mostly retrospective, with substantial risk of residual confounding; treatment allocation was frequently driven by performance status, life expectancy, disease extent, ascites, and clinician judgment. Third, individual patient data were unavailable, preventing reliable subgroup analyses by primary tumor, , ascites, peritoneal tumor burden, number and level of obstruction, performance status, or eligibility for disease-modifying systemic therapy. Therefore, the recommendations should be interpreted as weak, practice-oriented guidance based on the best available evidence and expert consensus rather than as definitive comparative-effectiveness conclusions.

Fourth, patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and quality-of-life data were not available in the included studies. No study used validated PRO instruments to assess symptom burden, functional recovery, treatment-related burden, time spent at home, stoma-related impact, caregiver burden, or patient preferences in patients with PSM-related MBO. This substantially limits the patient-centered interpretation of the available evidence, particularly in a frail population in whom decisions often require balancing short-term symptom relief, procedure-related morbidity, hospitalization burden, preservation of oncologic options, and goals of care.

Fifth, the available evidence includes heterogeneous tumor types, obstruction sites, treatment strategies, and clinical trajectories. As a result, the recommendations should be individualized according to primary tumor biology, performance status, expected prognosis, previous treatments, systemic therapy options, patient preferences, and local expertise. Moreover, although no age restriction was applied in the search strategy, no pediatric-specific evidence was identified. Therefore, the proposed algorithm should be interpreted primarily as guidance for adult patients.

Furthermore, ascites and peritoneal disease burden are clinically important because they influence technical feasibility, expected durability of palliation, postoperative risk, and suitability for systemic or intraperitoneal treatment. Some included studies, particularly in gastric outlet obstruction, reported ascites or carcinomatosis status, but definitions and reporting were inconsistent and aggregate data did not allow reliable ascites-based sensitivity analyses.

Future studies should stratify outcomes by ascites, peritoneal cancer index or equivalent disease-burden measures and primary tumor biology. Finally, they should incorporate standardized PRO measures and quality-of-life endpoints, in addition to traditional clinical outcomes such as morbidity, mortality, length of stay, obstruction resolution, and overall survival. Finally, the review was not prospectively registered in PROSPERO, although the PICO/PIRT questions, eligibility criteria, outcomes, and analytic approach were defined before screening.

Conclusions Despite the low certainty of the available evidence, this consensus-based framework provides a structured approach to support decision-making in emergency presentations of PSM-related MBO. The proposed diagnostic–therapeutic algorithm should be interpreted as practical guidance rather than a strong evidence-based mandate, and its recommendations should be applied through individualized multidisciplinary judgement, taking into account clinical stability, tumor biology, expected prognosis, patient preferences, goals of care, and local expertise.

The available evidence remains limited, but it is sufficient to support a structured emergency pathway for MBO in patients with PSM. Contrast-enhanced CT should be used to define anatomy and rule out urgent complications; in the absence of perforation, ischemia, shock, or peritonitis, a time-limited attempt at nonoperative management is appropriate; escalation to surgery or endoscopy should be individualized according to performance status, life expectancy, obstruction pattern, technical feasibility, and oncologic trajectory. The central message of these WSES-PSOGI-SICO guidelines is that patients with PSM presenting in emergency settings should not be managed as a homogeneous end-stage population. For selected patients, the acute decision can preserve or compromise subsequent oncologic options. The proposed algorithm offers a pragmatic framework for peripheral and referral hospitals while prospective, patient-centered research is developed.
